chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The best of the rows in prayer is the first one, and the best of the rows in funerals is the last one.' It was said, 'O Messenger of Allah, and why?' He said: 'Because it becomes a veil for the women.'

key_terms.الْمُؤَخَّرُ: the one who is behind/the last
key_terms.الْمُقَدَّمُ: the one who is in front/the first

ai.seo_question: What is the preferred position for rows in funeral mourners should take in the row during a funeral prayer?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the distinct jurisprudential etiquette (adab) for congregational prayer versus funeral processions, emphasizing the functional role of the rows. While the first row is prioritized for regular Salah to maximize devotion, the last row in Janazah serves a practical purpose as a 'sutra' (barrier) for women, reflecting the spatial dynamics of mixed-gender gatherings in early Islamic practice. This distinction underscores the Shia scholarly view that ritual excellence is often tied to context-specific wisdom rather than a single static rule.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Al Nowfaly, from Al Sakuny, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Rasool-Allahsaww said: ‘The best of the rows regarding the (Prescribed) Salaat is the first one, and the best of the rows regarding the funeral is the last one’. It was said, ‘O Rasool-Allahsaww! And why is it so?’ Hesaww said: ‘For it to become a veil for the women’.
en.sarwar: 3. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from al-Nawfaliy from al-Sakuniy who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, that the Messenger of Allah has said, ‘The best row in Salah (prayer) is the first row but the best row in Salah (prayer) for dead bodies is the last one.’ It was asked, ‘Why is it so, O Messenger of Allah?’ He (the Messenger of Allah) said, ‘It is a curtain for women.’”
